Welcome Letter

Dear Shareholders and Members,

At a time when political divisions seem to dominate nearly every conversation, we’ve been reflecting on something that has served the Suburban Realtors Alliance well throughout its history: our commitment to working with elected leaders on both sides of the aisle.

Within our own Realtor community, we have members who are passionate about their political beliefs, whether they identify as Republicans, Democrats, or Independents. But one thing that has always distinguished the SRA is that we’ve never allowed those differences to define our relationships with elected officials or interfere with our mission.

From the beginning, our advocacy has followed a simple philosophy: treat everyone with respect, build genuine relationships, and look for opportunities to find common ground and work together.

At the local level, where so many decisions affecting real estate transactions are made, we’ve developed productive relationships with elected officials and municipal staff across the political spectrum. We don’t approach a township supervisor or borough council member based on party affiliation. We approach them as potential partners in finding reasonable solutions.

That same philosophy guides our work alongside our state and national associations in Harrisburg and Washington, DC. One strong example is the Municipal Code and Ordinance Compliance Act (MCOCA). Working with legislators from both parties, the Pennsylvania Association of Realtors and SRA helped amend MCOCA in 2016, and strengthen it again in 2024. Those amendments were passed unanimously in both the House and Senate, and secured important protections for homebuyers and sellers, ensuring that municipal code violations found during use and occupancy inspections don’t block the sale of a home or unnecessarily delay settlement.

The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, passed just this year by Congress, is another example of sensible legislation, championed by Realtors, that garnered broad bipartisan support. It's a landmark federal statute with wide-ranging provisions designed to improve housing affordability nationwide.

Working in a spirit of bipartisanship doesn’t mean working without convictions. We hold strong positions on private property rights, housing development and affordability, municipal regulation, and the ability of Realtors to serve their clients. We advocate vigorously for those issues regardless of which party holds office.

We’ve also learned that lasting progress rarely comes from treating people who disagree as adversaries. More often, it comes from listening, understanding different perspectives, and actively finding common ground.

As we look back on 2026, we’re proud not only of what SRA has accomplished, but of how we accomplished it. Our effectiveness has always depended on the relationships we’ve built, the credibility we’ve established over many years, and the trust we’ve earned across the political spectrum.

In a world that increasingly encourages us to choose sides, we believe there’s real value in choosing instead to work together. It’s an approach that has served the SRA and our members for many years, and one that will continue to guide our work in the years ahead.

Sincerely,

Jamie Ridge
CEO/President
Scott Freeman
Board Chair

About SRA

The Suburban REALTORS® Alliance is a government-affairs office serving Realtors in the Philadelphia suburbs.

We have two shareholder associations:

&

Mission

The SRA’s mission is to impact public policy for the benefit of real estate and the protection of private property rights.

History

SRA was founded in 1998 as the Realtors Legislative Alliance. In 2006, the organization rebranded as the Suburban Realtors Alliance. Today, the SRA represents more than 13,000 members across 238 municipalities in Bucks, Chester, Delaware and Montgomery counties.

Where our members live

2026 Notes

  1. Trends

    Municipalities focus on data center zoning

    Across our region and throughout the nation, local governments moved quickly to enact zoning regulations for data centers. Massive projects have already been proposed in places like Trainer, Limerick, Upper Merion, East Whiteland, and Falls. As the artificial intelligence industry booms, residents and local officials are trying to constrain data centers’ negative impacts, such as noise, water and energy usage, and pollution.

    We have also continued to see earned income taxes spread, as local governments look to diversify their tax bases.

    Short-term rental ordinances faded as a hot topic in 2026, though municipalities continued to regulate them in places like Kennett Square. The controversy over the acquisition of local sewer systems by larger corporations also quieted down compared to recent years, though control of the Chester Water Authority continued to be litigated in court.

  2. March 2026

    Speaking to Students

    In March, Jamie Ridge spoke to seniors from Archbishop Wood Catholic High School during their visit to the Bucks County Association of Realtors office. The students heard from association leaders and industry professionals about leadership, market trends and career opportunities.

  3. April 2026

    Warwick Township amends use and occupancy ordinance

    Warwick Township passed an amended version of its use and occupancy ordinance, placing more emphasis on missing and incomplete construction permits. The SRA shared concerns about the ordinance with the township manager and solicitor, and reminded the township that missing permits found during a resale inspection still fall under the protection of the Municipal Code and Ordinance Compliance Act, and buyers should be allowed to correct the violation within 12 months after settlement.

  4. April 30, 2026

    PA Supreme Court rules stormwater fee is a tax

    The Pennsylvania Supreme Court issued a long-awaited decision on West Chester Borough’s stormwater program, finding the borough’s stream protection fee is a tax and not a fee. The decision means West Chester University — a nontaxable entity — is not obligated to pay the tax. The ruling has wide-reaching implications, as all municipalities struggle to manage stormwater issues. Middletown Township, Bucks County, for example, proactively refunded a local nonprofit senior living facility for its stormwater impact fee payments.

  5. July 2026

    Skippack Township adopts rental ordinance

    Skippack Township adopted a new rental ordinance in July following several months of review and SRA stakeholder input. The final ordinance included three notable improvements made after board member Eric Rehling’s meeting with township officials. The township eliminated the proposed three-unrelated-persons occupancy cap and the strict classification of cousins as unrelated persons; reduced occupant reporting from quarterly to semi-annually; and adopted a separate resolution establishing a transparent, flat $100 fee for each rental license transaction. These changes addressed several of the Alliance’s concerns regarding occupancy restrictions, administrative burdens on property owners, and an initially open-ended fee structure.

  6. July 2026

    PAR’s first statewide local GAD and field rep summit

    Jamie Ridge and Erin Smist attended PAR’s first statewide local GAD and field rep summit in Lititz in July. Local GADs and field representatives attended presentations by PAR CEO Mike McGee, chief advocacy officer Sherri Martin and her staff, and panel discussions conducted by local GADs and field reps. Jamie took the stage for a panel focused on demonstrating the value of government affairs advocacy to Realtor members.

  7. July 2026

    21st Century ROAD to Housing Act becomes law

    The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a landmark piece of bipartisan legislation championed by the National Association of Realtors, was passed by Congress on June 23 and became law on July 11. The legislation marked the culmination of one of NAR’s largest coordinated advocacy campaigns in recent years. NAR’s Federal Political Coordinators (FPCs) played a key role in informing legislators about how the bill would ease the housing crisis. Rather than advocating for a single proposal, NAR worked to assemble broad bipartisan support for dozens of complementary policies that together address the nation’s housing shortage from multiple angles. The legislation focuses on four broad priorities: increasing housing supply, expanding access to homeownership, expanding access to capital, and supporting veterans.

  8. August 2026

    Upper Darby adopts lead-poisoning-prevention ordinance

    Upper Darby Township adopted a lead-poisoning-prevention ordinance requiring pre-1978 rental properties, homes at the time of transfer, and child care facilities to be certified as lead safe or lead free. Recognizing that the ordinance had sufficient council support for passage, the Alliance focused its advocacy on ensuring that the final requirements comply with the Municipal Code and Ordinance Compliance Act (MCOCA), preserve an owner’s choice between lead-safe and lead-free certification, and ensure that the presence of lead does not prevent occupancy through issuance of a temporary access permit.

  9. August 2026

    Wrightstown passes sewer lateral ordinance

    Wrightstown Township supervisors passed a sewer lateral inspection ordinance despite SRA concerns that several provisions conflict with the Pennsylvania Municipal Code and Ordinance Compliance Act (MCOCA). The township solicitor acknowledged SRA’s concerns but recommended adoption because the ordinance had already been advertised, with amendments to follow. The ordinance requires repair escrows, mandates repairs within 60 days or by settlement, and allows the township to withhold a resale certificate until repairs are completed — provisions that conflict with MCOCA. SRA staff is following up with the township to bring the ordinance into compliance.

  10. October 2026

    SB 838 becomes Act 100

    Gov. Josh Shapiro signed Senate Bill 838 into law as Act 100. The bill, which passed both the Pennsylvania House and Senate unanimously, was a priority for the Pennsylvania Association of Realtors during the legislative session. It amends the Private Licensed Schools Act to clarify that real estate and appraiser schools are exempt. The new law ensures that the schools are not subject to duplicative regulation and fees within the commonwealth, as they are already regulated by the Department of State.

  11. Oct. 23, 2026

    Affordable Housing webinar

    Jamie Ridge moderated a webinar hosted by the BCAR DEI Committee on Oct. 23. The panelists — Realtors Monique Simpson and Drew Amin and housing counselor Sherry Pace — discussed barriers to homeownership, practical strategies for guiding clients, and the latest market and policy developments affecting affordability.

  12. Year-round

    Greeting new members

    SRA staff members are fortunate to speak to new members for about 15 minutes during their orientation sessions at BCAR and Tri-County. Whether virtually or in-person, new members hear the basics of local governance and how it relates to the use and occupancy process.

Local Advocacy

SRA often engages directly at the municipal level to influence policy broadly, or in specific situations involving our members.

Here are a few highlights from 2026.

Bucks County

Working together with Upper Southampton officials to protect sellers and buyers

Protecting property owners sometimes means challenging existing municipal policies. Other times, it means working with local officials to prevent problems before they begin.

That’s what the Suburban Realtors Alliance has been doing in Upper Southampton Township, where a proposed resale use-and-occupancy ordinance raised concerns about compliance with Pennsylvania’s Municipal Code and Ordinance Compliance Act (MCOCA).

The SRA discovered the proposal through a legal notice in a local newspaper and immediately began reviewing it. Board member and attorney Alex Shnayder, who has extensive knowledge of municipal inspections and MCOCA, provided additional legal insight.

After identifying several potentially problematic provisions in the draft ordinance, including requirements that could delay settlements over outstanding violations and missing construction permits, the SRA sent its concerns to the township manager and solicitor.

Township officials responded positively, agreeing to table the ordinance while revisions were made.

A second draft included significant improvements, incorporating MCOCA’s definitions and requirements for issuing full, temporary, and temporary access certificates. However, questions remained about a separate resale certificate requiring seller disclosures and other provisions affecting property transfers.

The SRA continued its discussions, culminating in a productive meeting with the township solicitor, manager and codes official, who were receptive to our recommendations.

Although another draft is pending, township officials have invited the SRA to address the ordinance at an upcoming public meeting.

The Upper Southampton experience demonstrates how proactive advocacy and constructive relationships with local government can protect property owners, prevent unnecessary settlement delays, and promote municipal ordinances that comply with state law.

Chester County

NIMBYs vs. YIMBYs on the frontlines in Chester County

The battle over housing development in Chester County is intensifying, with two competing groups on the frontlines of the debate: NIMBYs (Not in My Backyard) and YIMBYs (Yes in My Backyard).

An October Philadelphia Inquirer article highlighted how organized groups of residents are raising money, hiring attorneys and mobilizing opposition to proposed developments throughout the county. In West Brandywine Township, residents have organized against a proposed 230-home development. Meanwhile, in West Whiteland Township, officials rejected a proposal to transform the shuttered Exton Square Mall into a walkable, mixed-use community with more than 700 homes, despite a favorable recommendation from the township’s planning commission. In this case, as in many others, the fight has moved into the courts.

These battles illustrate a growing tension in one of Pennsylvania’s most desirable counties: How do we preserve open space while making room for smart growth that can accommodate families who want to live and work in the county?

Chester County has long favored open-space preservation over housing development. But protecting open space and providing more affordable housing need not be mutually exclusive. Thoughtful planning that emphasizes higher-density development in appropriate locations, and a wider variety of housing options can help accomplish both goals.

Pennsylvania’s fragmented system of local government makes that balance difficult. Chester County has 73 municipalities, each with its own zoning authority. Even well-planned housing proposals can face fierce opposition from vocal NIMBY groups, leaving local officials under pressure to reject projects that could help address a countywide housing shortage.

Meanwhile, a growing number of organizations are making the case for more affordable housing. Groups such as Allies for Housing in Chester County, Habitat for Humanity of Chester County, the Suburban Realtors Alliance, and the Chester County Chamber of Business and Industry are advocating for more affordable and workforce housing options.

The stakes are significant. Young families, first-time homebuyers, teachers, first responders and other essential workers are struggling to afford housing in the communities they serve.

“At the SRA we believe that local governments need to balance legitimate community concerns with the urgent need for more affordable housing,” said Jamie Ridge, CEO of the SRA. “Chester County’s future depends not simply on preserving what makes it a desirable place to live, but also on ensuring that future generations can afford to call it home.”

Delaware County

SRA helps Collingdale Borough improve sewer lateral ordinance

Earlier this year when Collingdale Borough proposed a new sewer lateral inspection, SRA’s review raised immediate concerns. Several provisions appeared outdated and inconsistent with Pennsylvania’s Municipal Code and Ordinance Compliance Act (MCOCA), which protects property owners and buyers from municipal requirements that delay or disrupt real estate settlements.

The original proposal required sellers to correct sewer lateral defects before the borough would certify a property, potentially delaying or preventing settlement. It also failed to clearly establish the temporary certificates required under MCOCA or recognize the law's 12-month period for buyers to complete repairs after settlement. These provisions could have created significant obstacles for property owners and Realtors.

Fortunately, SRA had recently worked with neighboring Folcroft Borough on a sewer lateral ordinance that addressed these concerns while allowing the municipality to meet its inspection and state-mandated goals to stop inflow and infiltration from entering the sewer system through old infrastructure. We believed the Folcroft ordinance could serve as a useful model for Collingdale.

Drawing on established relationships with municipal solicitors in both boroughs, SRA reached out to share our concerns and recommend that Collingdale consider the approach adopted in Folcroft.

The response was positive and constructive. Working together, the municipal solicitors reviewed the proposed ordinance and incorporated important provisions from the Folcroft model to ensure compliance with MCOCA. Several weeks later, Collingdale Borough Council adopted the revised ordinance.

The experience illustrates an important aspect of SRA’s municipal advocacy efforts. Local officials are often working to address legitimate concerns about infrastructure and public safety, but proposed regulations can sometimes conflict with existing state laws that govern real estate transactions.

By identifying potential problems before an ordinance is adopted, and utilizing relationships that have been formed through the years, SRA can help communities achieve their goals while protecting and preserving property rights and real estate transactions.

The Collingdale experience is another example of how cooperation, communications, and the SRA’s reputation in the region can produce better outcomes for municipalities, our members, and the consumers they serve.

Montgomery County

Turning a settlement problem into a model solution

A last-minute problem with a real estate settlement in West Norriton Township could lead to a model improvement for how municipalities conduct resale use-and-occupancy inspections.

The Suburban Realtors Alliance learned of the issue from broker and Tri-County Suburban Realtors board member Lou Muscella, whose agent was informed by a township code official that no U&O certificate of any kind would be issued until all required property repairs were complete.

The illegal requirement forced the buyer to make repairs to a home before taking ownership — precisely the kind of situation Pennsylvania’s Municipal Code and Ordinance Compliance Act (MCOCA) was designed to prevent.

MCOCA requires municipalities to issue one of three certificates following a resale inspection, allowing settlements to proceed while providing purchasers up to 12 months to correct identified violations.

Following the settlement, the SRA immediately contacted the township manager and solicitor to explain the problem and request corrective action.

The township solicitor, with whom the SRA has successfully worked on previous issues, responded quickly, developing a comprehensive new application and inspection process designed to ensure compliance with MCOCA.

The proposed procedures clearly distinguish between ordinary and substantial code violations, establish the appropriate certificate requirements, identify commonly inspected items and their corresponding township code provisions, and recognize the statutory 12-month correction period.

The SRA welcomed the draft and recommended several additional improvements, which the solicitor is now incorporating.

Once finalized, West Norriton’s new procedures could serve as a model for municipalities throughout southeastern Pennsylvania and beyond.

The experience demonstrates how the SRA’s relationships with Realtors and municipal officials can turn an individual settlement problem into lasting improvements for property owners and the real estate industry.

News Briefs

SRA publishes weekly regional news briefs covering local government and real estate policy throughout the Philadelphia suburbs. In 2026, we transitioned to a new email marketing platform, Brevo, saving money and adding back-end features like link-click heat maps.

Local news is changing.

In 2026, the Chester County Press quietly ceased operations.
It had been a consistent source of southern Chesco news. Across the region, established papers are consolidating, shrinking and vanishing.
Online sources are taking root.
Local news outlets are sprouting throughout the region, employing an array of approaches to local news. Some of them have consistently offered reliable, well-sourced information and seem to be gaining local advertisers.
Garbage sites are muddying the waters.
Error-filled, AI-powered websites with little human oversight are spreading like invasive vines.

We’re adapting.

We’ve expanded our research to include more primary sources.

There are hundreds posted each day. We scan for the few that impact real estate.

Grassroots

Day on the Hill

On June 3, 275 Pennsylvania Realtors, including more than 60 members from the Bucks County Association of Realtors and Tri-County Suburban Realtors, attended more than 100 meetings with legislators at the Capitol in Harrisburg during the Pennsylvania Association of Realtors annual PA Realtor Day on the Hill.

They advocated for three key bills related to homeownership and real estate in the commonwealth: SB 838 – Private Licensed School Act Amendment; HB 1095 – Sealing of Eviction Records; and SB 907 – Licensure of Home Inspectors.

RPAC

The Realtors Political Action Committee (RPAC) helps elect officials who support homeownership and the real estate industry. In southeastern Pennsylvania, RPAC activities are facilitated by SERPAC — Southeast Realtors Political Action Committee.

In the 2026 general election, RPAC trustees met with several candidates for state office and supported 32 candidates.
